Text: As a medical abbreviation, ED can stand for {{c1::emergency department, erectile dysfunction}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As emergency department: "transporting emergent to the ED" — the ER, EMS's usual destination for acute patients.
  2. As erectile dysfunction: ED treated with sildenafil (Viagra) — never give nitroglycerin if taken recently (dangerous hypotension).
  3. As emergency department: "boarding in the ED" — the department holding an admitted patient until an inpatient bed opens.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::EDC}} stands for {{c2::estimated date of confinement}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "G2P1 at 38 weeks, EDC in two weeks by first-trimester ultrasound."
  2. Radio report: "Active labor, contractions 3 minutes apart, EDC in two days."
  3. Handoff: "32 weeks by EDC, presenting with vaginal bleeding."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::EEG}} stands for {{c2::electroencephalogram}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Neuro recommends EEG to characterize the seizure activity."
  2. Charting: "Continuous EEG started to rule out nonconvulsive status epilepticus."
  3. Handoff: "EEG ordered to work up persistent altered mental status."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::EKG}} stands for {{c2::electrocardiogram}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "EKG showing wide-complex tachycardia at 180, pt hypotensive."
  2. Charting: "12-lead EKG unremarkable, no acute ST changes."
  3. Handoff: "Serial EKGs stable, troponin pending, pain resolved after nitro."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ENT}} stands for {{c2::ears, nose, and throat}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Peritonsillar abscess drained, ENT consulted for follow-up."
  2. Charting: "Epistaxis unresponsive to pressure, nares packed and referred to ENT."
  3. Radio report: "Foreign body lodged in the throat, may need ENT at your facility."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::EOC}} stands for {{c2::Emergency Operations Center}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Requesting mutual aid through the county EOC for the interstate pileup."
  2. Charting: "Mass casualty incident coordinated through the regional EOC."
  3. Handoff: "EOC activated for the hurricane response, staging at the fairgrounds."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ER}} stands for {{c2::emergency room}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "ETA 5 minutes to the ER, requesting a trauma bay."
  2. Charting: "Pt advised to return to the ER if symptoms worsen; refused transport."
  3. Handoff: "Transferring care to the ER charge nurse, report given."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ET, ETT}} stands for {{c2::endotracheal, endotracheal tube}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "ET intubation successful, 7.5 ETT, 22 cm at the teeth."
  2. Radio report: "ETT confirmed by waveform capnography and equal breath sounds."
  3. Handoff: "ETT secured at 22 cm, recheck placement after every move."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ETA}} stands for {{c2::estimated time of arrival}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "STEMI activation, ETA to your ED 8 minutes."
  2. Dispatch: "Launching air medical, helicopter ETA 12 minutes."
  3. Radio report: "Critical trauma inbound, ETA 5 minutes, activate the trauma team."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ETCO2}} stands for {{c2::end-tidal carbon dioxide}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Post-intubation ETCO2 38 with square waveform, tube confirmed."
  2. During arrest: "ETCO2 only 8, coaching crew to push harder and faster."
  3. Handoff: "Sudden ETCO2 jump to 42 tipped us off to ROSC."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ETOH}} stands for {{c2::ethyl alcohol}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Found down, strong ETOH odor, GCS 13, airway patent."
  2. Handoff: "Chronic ETOH use, watch for withdrawal seizures overnight."
  3. Radio report: "Acute ETOH intoxication, protecting airway, transporting emergent."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::°F}} stands for {{c2::degrees Fahrenheit}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Temp 103.4°F, flushed and diaphoretic, fluids started."
  2. Handoff: "Febrile at 101.2°F, sepsis workup underway."
  3. Charting: "Hypothermic at 94.1°F, applying warm blankets and heat."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::FIO2}} stands for {{c2::fraction of inspired oxygen}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Titrate FIO2 down to keep sats 94-98%."
  2. Charting: "Preoxygenating at FIO2 100% before intubation attempt."
  3. Handoff: "Vent set to FIO2 40%, PEEP 5, sats holding 97%."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::FBS}} stands for {{c2::fasting blood sugar}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "FBS 142 mg/dL, consistent with new-onset diabetes."
  2. Order: "Draw FBS in the morning before any breakfast."
  3. Handoff: "Elevated FBS on labs, endocrine consult requested."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::Fe}} stands for {{c2::iron}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Start oral Fe supplement for iron-deficiency anemia."
  2. Charting: "Low serum Fe, chronic fatigue and pallor now explained."
  3. Radio report: "Pediatric Fe overdose, ingested adult iron pills, poison control contacted."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::FHR}} stands for {{c2::fetal heart rate}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "FHR 140 by Doppler, reassuring for the fetus."
  2. Radio report: "Term OB patient, FHR in the 150s, contractions 3 minutes apart."
  3. Handoff: "FHR dipped to 90 with contractions, expediting to L&D."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::FHx}} stands for {{c2::family history}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "FHx positive for early MI, father at 45."
  2. Charting: "Left-sided weakness with FHx of early stroke."
  3. Handoff: "FHx of sudden cardiac death, low threshold for cardiac workup."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::fl. fld}} stands for {{c2::fluid}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "500 mL NS IV fld bolus, then reassess lungs."
  2. Charting: "Poor oral fld intake x3 days, membranes dry, skin tenting."
  3. Handoff: "Free fld on the FAST exam, trauma surgery aware."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::fx}} stands for {{c2::fracture}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Deformed forearm, likely closed fx, distal pulses intact."
  2. Charting: "Open tibia fx, bleeding controlled, splinted in position."
  3. Handoff: "Suspected hip fx, leg shortened and externally rotated."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GB}} stands for {{c2::gallbladder}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "RUQ pain after a fatty meal, GB pathology suspected."
  2. Handoff: "Positive Murphy's sign, GB ultrasound ordered."
  3. Charting: "Post-op day 1 status post GB removal, tolerating diet."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GCS}} stands for {{c2::Glasgow Coma Scale}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Head injury, GCS 8, intubating for airway protection."
  2. Charting: "GCS 15 on arrival, eye, verbal, and motor all intact."
  3. Handoff: "GCS dropped from 14 to 10, repeat head CT ordered."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GERD}} stands for {{c2::gastroesophageal reflux disease}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Burning chest pain, likely GERD, ruling out cardiac first."
  2. Handoff: "History of GERD, discomfort relieved with antacids."
  3. Charting: "GERD flare, sour taste and cough worse lying flat."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GI}} stands for {{c2::gastrointestinal}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "62 y/o M c/o GI upset, N/V/D x2 days, denies hematochezia."
  2. Radio report: "Upper GI bleed, coffee-ground emesis, BP 88/54, starting fluids."
  3. Handoff: "Lower GI bleed workup, guaiac-positive stool, GI consult in."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GSW}} stands for {{c2::gunshot wound}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "19 y/o M, single GSW to left chest, hypotensive, ETA 4."
  2. Charting: "GSW with entrance wound to RLQ, no exit wound identified."
  3. Handoff: "Multiple GSWs to abdomen, taken straight to the OR."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::gtt}} stands for {{c2::drop(s)}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Proparacaine 2 gtt to right eye before foreign-body removal."
  2. Order: "Latanoprost 1 gtt to affected eye at bedtime."
  3. Charting: "Macrodrip IV set running at 15 gtt/min."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GTT}} stands for {{c2::glucose tolerance test}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Scheduled for GTT to work up new-onset hyperglycemia."
  2. Handoff: "Failed the 1-hr glucose screen at 28 wks, sent for the 3-hr GTT."
  3. Charting: "GTT confirmed type 2 DM, started on metformin."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::GU}} stands for {{c2::genitourinary}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "GU exam deferred, pt reports dysuria and left flank pain."
  2. Radio report: "Blunt GU trauma, gross hematuria following the MVC."
  3. Handoff: "Admitted for GU workup, recurrent UTIs with hematuria."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::gyn}} stands for {{c2::gynecology}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Referred to gyn for abnormal uterine bleeding."
  2. Handoff: "OB/gyn consulted for possible ectopic, hCG pending."
  3. Charting: "Gyn hx significant for PCOS and endometriosis."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::h}} stands for {{c2::hour}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Ondansetron 4 mg IV q6h PRN nausea."
  2. Charting: "Chest pain onset approx 2 h prior to arrival, at rest."
  3. Order: "Neuro checks q1h overnight."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::H&P}} stands for {{c2::history and physical}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Full H&P completed and documented on admission."
  2. Handoff: "H&P unremarkable aside from the new systolic murmur."
  3. Order: "Admit to medicine, H&P by the on-call team tonight."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HA, H/A}} stands for {{c2::headache}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Pt c/o sudden severe HA, 'worst of my life.'"
  2. Radio report: "Thunderclap HA, concerned for subarachnoid bleed."
  3. Handoff: "H/A resolved after Toradol and fluids, discharged home."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::Hb, Hgb}} stands for {{c2::hemoglobin}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Hgb 7.1, transfusing 2 units PRBCs."
  2. Handoff: "Hb dropped from 12 to 8 overnight, ?GI source."
  3. Charting: "Baseline Hgb 9 with known chronic anemia."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HBV}} stands for {{c2::hepatitis B virus}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Needlestick exposure, source patient HBV positive."
  2. Handoff: "Chronic HBV on tenofovir, LFTs trending down."
  3. Charting: "HBV vaccine series complete, titers confirmed protective."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::Hct}} stands for {{c2::hematocrit}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Hct 21%, actively resuscitating with blood products."
  2. Handoff: "Serial Hct stable at 30, no evidence of ongoing bleed."
  3. Charting: "Hct 24%, consistent with acute blood loss."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HCV}} stands for {{c2::hepatitis C virus}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Hx of HCV related to prior IV drug use."
  2. Handoff: "HCV cleared after a course of DAAs, now cured."
  3. Charting: "Cirrhosis secondary to chronic HCV infection."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HH}} stands for {{c2::hiatal hernia}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "CXR incidentally revealed a large HH."
  2. Handoff: "Known HH presenting with chronic reflux and regurgitation."
  3. Charting: "Sliding HH confirmed on barium swallow."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HIV}} stands for {{c2::human immunodeficiency virus}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "HIV positive, on ART, last CD4 count 550."
  2. Charting: "Occupational needlestick, initiating HIV PEP protocol."
  3. Handoff: "Newly diagnosed HIV, started on antiretroviral therapy."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::H 2O}} stands for {{c2::water}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Flush the feeding tube with 30 mL H2O after each med."
  2. Vent settings: "PEEP set at 5 cmH2O, plateau pressure 22."
  3. Charting: "Dehydrated with dry mucosa; encouraging PO H2O intake."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HPI}} stands for {{c2::history of present illness}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "HPI: 58 y/o M c/o crushing chest pain x45 min radiating to jaw, diaphoretic."
  2. Handoff: "Her HPI is 3 days of worsening cough, fever, now pleuritic chest pain."
  3. Charting: "HPI: sudden 'worst headache of life' while straining, peaked in seconds."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HR}} stands for {{c2::heart rate}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Vitals: HR 138 and regular, BP 90/60, sats 94%."
  2. Charting: "HR 42 with associated dizziness; atropine on standby."
  3. Handoff: "Post-cardioversion, HR now 78 and regular."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::hr}} stands for {{c2::hour}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "C/o abdominal pain x6 hr, progressively worsening."
  2. Order: "Repeat troponin in 3 hr."
  3. Charting: "Last known well 2 hr ago per family."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::HTN}} stands for {{c2::hypertension}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "PMHx: HTN, T2DM, prior MI."
  2. Radio report: "BP 220/120 in known HTN, concern for hypertensive emergency."
  3. Charting: "Reports HTN but ran out of lisinopril 5 days ago."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::Hx}} stands for {{c2::history}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Cardiac Hx significant for CABG in 2019."
  2. Charting: "Denies any Hx of seizures or head trauma."
  3. Charting: "Social Hx: 1 ppd smoker x20 years."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::I&O}} stands for {{c2::intake and output}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Strict I&O; notify provider if output drops below 30 mL/hr."
  2. Charting: "12-hr I&O: in 1000 mL, out 1400 mL, net negative 400."
  3. Handoff: "Monitoring I&O closely on this CHF exacerbation."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ICP}} stands for {{c2::intracranial pressure}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Head injury with Cushing's triad, worried about rising ICP."
  2. Order: "Elevate head of bed 30 degrees to help lower ICP."
  3. Charting: "GCS dropping with a blown pupil, concern for increased ICP."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, ICS can stand for {{c1::incident command system, intercostal space}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As intercostal space: needle decompression at the 2nd ICS, midclavicular line — relieving a tension pneumothorax between the ribs.
  2. As incident command system: "ICS established, I have Command" — the NIMS structure organizing a multi-casualty scene.
  3. As intercostal space: chest tube in the 5th ICS, anterior axillary line — draining a hemothorax; count down the ribs.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::ICU}} stands for {{c2::intensive care unit}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Handoff: "Direct admit to the ICU for vasopressors and vent management."
  2. Charting: "Transferred from ED to ICU after intubation."
  3. Radio report: "Critical STEMI, will need an ICU bed after the cath lab."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IDDM}} stands for {{c2::insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "PMHx: IDDM on an insulin pump."
  2. Radio report: "Known IDDM, glucose 42 and altered, giving oral glucose."
  3. Handoff: "IDDM in DKA, Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IM}} stands for {{c2::intramuscular}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the lateral thigh for anaphylaxis."
  2. Order: "Glucagon 1 mg IM for hypoglycemia with no IV access."
  3. Charting: "Ketorolac 30 mg IM administered for acute back pain."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IMS}} stands for {{c2::incident management system}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Multi-vehicle MCI, activating IMS, I'll assume Command."
  2. Charting: "Scene run under IMS with triage, treatment, and transport groups."
  3. Handoff: "Under IMS you report to the Medical Branch Director."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IN}} stands for {{c2::intranasal}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Naloxone 4 mg IN, single spray to one nostril, suspected opioid OD."
  2. Order: "Midazolam IN to break the active seizure, no IV access."
  3. Charting: "Administered fentanyl IN via atomizer for the child's fracture pain."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IO}} stands for {{c2::intraosseous}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Two failed IV sticks, go for an IO in the proximal tibia."
  2. Radio report: "Arrest with IO access in place, pushing epi q3-5 min."
  3. Charting: "Humeral IO placed for fluid resuscitation in profound shock."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IUD}} stands for {{c2::intrauterine device (contraceptive)}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "GYN Hx: hormonal IUD in place since 2024."
  2. Charting: "Reproductive-age F, pelvic pain, IUD present, test to r/o ectopic."
  3. Handoff: "Lower abd pain with IUD, GYN to evaluate for displacement or PID."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::IV}} stands for {{c2::intravenous}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Established 18g IV in right AC, NS running at TKO."
  2. Order: "Push 1 mg atropine IV, may repeat q3-5 min for bradycardia."
  3. Radio report: "Two large-bore IVs placed, fluids wide open for the hypotension."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::JVD}} stands for {{c2::jugular venous distention}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Neck: +JVD at 45 degrees, trachea midline."
  2. Radio report: "Hypotensive with JVD and muffled heart tones, concerned for tamponade."
  3. Handoff: "New JVD with bilateral crackles, treating as CHF exacerbation."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::kg}} stands for {{c2::kilogram}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "Peds patient roughly 20 kg, requesting weight-based orders."
  2. Order: "Fentanyl 1 mcg/kg IV for pain control."
  3. Charting: "Pt weight 80 kg per family; all doses calculated accordingly."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, LE can stand for {{c1::lower extremity, left eye, lupus erythematosus}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As lower extremity: "unilateral LE swelling and calf pain" — think DVT; also how you chart leg trauma or edema.
  2. As lupus erythematosus: SLE (systemic LE) — autoimmune disease with a malar rash, joint pain, and multi-organ involvement.
  3. As left eye: "foreign body, LE" — documenting the left eye (though OS is the more common shorthand).

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::LLL}} stands for {{c2::left lower lobe of the lung}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Diminished breath sounds with crackles in the LLL."
  2. Radio report: "Febrile with productive cough, suspect LLL pneumonia."
  3. Handoff: "CXR confirmed LLL infiltrate, antibiotics started in the ED."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::LLQ}} stands for {{c2::left lower quadrant of the abdomen}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Abd soft, tender to palpation in the LLQ."
  2. Radio report: "Severe LLQ pain with guarding, query diverticulitis."
  3. Handoff: "LLQ tenderness with rebound, surgery consulted."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::L/m, LPM}} stands for {{c2::liters per minute}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Oxygen at 15 LPM via non-rebreather mask."
  2. Charting: "Placed on nasal cannula at 2 L/m, sats up to 97%."
  3. Radio report: "Maintaining sats on 6 LPM, no respiratory distress."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::LMP}} stands for {{c2::last menstrual period}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "LMP approximately 6 weeks ago per patient."
  2. Radio report: "Abd pain, LMP two months ago, considering ectopic."
  3. Handoff: "Reproductive-age female, LMP uncertain, hCG pending."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, LOC can stand for {{c1::level of consciousness, loss of consciousness}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As level of consciousness: "declining LOC, GCS now 10" — how alert the patient is (AVPU/GCS); a drop means deterioration.
  2. As loss of consciousness: "syncope with brief LOC" — the patient fainted; a discrete pass-out event.
  3. As loss of consciousness: "+LOC after the MVC" — did they black out on impact? A key concussion/TBI triage question.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::LUL}} stands for {{c2::left upper lobe of the lung}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Breath sounds clear bilaterally except diminished in the LUL."
  2. Radio report: "Gunshot to left chest, absent breath sounds over the LUL."
  3. Handoff: "LUL mass on CT, pulmonology referral placed."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::LUQ}} stands for {{c2::left upper quadrant of the abdomen}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "LUQ tenderness after blunt trauma, query splenic injury."
  2. Radio report: "Restrained driver with LUQ pain, concern for the spleen."
  3. Handoff: "LUQ pain radiating to left shoulder, positive Kehr sign."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::LVAD}} stands for {{c2::left ventricular assist device}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Hx of end-stage heart failure, LVAD placed 2023."
  2. Radio report: "LVAD patient, no palpable pulse, obtaining MAP by Doppler."
  3. Handoff: "LVAD low-flow alarm sounding, VAD coordinator en route."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::MAE}} stands for {{c2::moves all extremities}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "Neuro: alert, MAE, no focal deficits."
  2. Handoff: "Postictal on arrival, now MAE with full strength."
  3. Radio report: "Trauma patient GCS 15, MAE, no obvious deformity."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::MAEW}} stands for {{c2::moves all extremities well}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "A&Ox4, MAEW, sensation intact in all four extremities."
  2. Handoff: "Fall from standing, MAEW, denies numbness or tingling."
  3. Radio report: "Restrained driver, ambulatory on scene, MAEW."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::mg}} stands for {{c2::milligram}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Aspirin 324 mg PO, have the patient chew it."
  2. Charting: "Gave 4 mg ondansetron IV for nausea."
  3. Radio report: "Requesting orders for 2 mg morphine IV for pain."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::MI}} stands for {{c2::myocardial infarction}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "12-lead shows STEMI, activating the cath lab for acute MI."
  2. Charting: "Hx of prior MI in 2019 with stent placement."
  3. Handoff: "Ruling out MI, first troponin negative, serial enzymes ordered."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, MICU can stand for {{c1::mobile intensive care unit; medical intensive care unit}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As mobile intensive care unit: the MICU rig — a paramedic-level ambulance equipped to deliver critical care in the field.
  2. As medical intensive care unit: "admitted to the MICU" — the hospital ICU for sepsis, DKA, and respiratory failure (vs the surgical SICU).
  3. As mobile intensive care unit: "MICU transport" — a critical-care crew moving an intubated, drip-dependent patient between hospitals.

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::min}} stands for {{c2::minute}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Recheck vitals q5 min en route."
  2. Charting: "Reassessed pain 20 min after morphine, now 3/10."
  3. Radio report: "ETA approximately 8 min to your facility."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::mL}} stands for {{c2::milliliter}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Order: "Ondansetron 4 mg (2 mL) slow IV push for nausea."
  2. Charting: "250 mL normal saline bolus given, lungs remained clear."
  3. Handoff: "Put out 30 mL urine in the last hour, so still oliguric."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::mm}} stands for {{c2::millimeter}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Charting: "3 cm laceration, ~5 mm deep, to left forearm; controlled with direct pressure."
  2. Radio report: "Pupils equal at 4 mm, reactive to light."
  3. Handoff: "ST elevation of about 2 mm in the inferior leads on the 12-lead."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::mm Hg}} stands for {{c2::millimeters of mercury}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. Radio report: "BP 88/50 mm Hg, hypotensive, starting a fluid bolus."
  2. Charting: "BP 210/118 mm Hg with a severe headache, hypertensive emergency."
  3. Handoff: "Pressure came up to 116/72 mm Hg after the second liter."

Text: The abbreviation {{c1::MOI}} stands for {{c2::mechanism of injury}}.
Back Extra:
WHEN YOU'D USE IT

  2. Charting: "MOI is a fall from a 20-foot roof onto concrete."

Text: As a medical abbreviation, NAD can stand for {{c1::no apparent distress, no appreciable disease}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: this abbreviation has several distinct meanings; read it in context.

WHEN YOU'D USE IT
  1. As no apparent distress: "alert, resting comfortably, in NAD" — the classic general-appearance line; the patient looks well.
  2. As no apparent distress: "post-nebulizer, breathing easy, now in NAD" — documenting relief after treatment.
  3. As no appreciable disease: "chest film: NAD" — the imaging or exam read as normal, nothing pathologic found.
